lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Metal casting is one of the oldest and most useful trades in the world. In Africa, foundries have been shaping metal for centuriesâfrom the bronze casters of Benin to the iron smelters of the Haya people in Tanzania. Today, the demand for cast metal parts is everywhere: water pumps, grinding mills, car parts, cooking stoves, farm tools, and construction fittings. If you can melt metal and pour it into a mould, you can make money solving real problems in your community.

Starting a foundry does not require a huge factory. Many successful African foundries began in a backyard with a simple charcoal furnace, a few crucibles, and locally sourced scrap metal. The key is to learn the basics: how to build a furnace that reaches the right temperature, how to prepare sand moulds that don't crack, and how to pour safely. You also need to understand the business side: what parts are in demand, how to price your work, and how to find customers.

In this module, you will learn the foundations of the foundry business. We will cover the tools you need, the step-by-step process of making a casting, common mistakes and how to fix them, safety practices that keep you alive and healthy, and a practical exercise to get your hands dirty. By the end, you will have the knowledge to start small and grow. Remember, every big foundry started with a single pour. Your first casting might be a simple hoe blade or a cooking pot handle. That's fine. What matters is that you start, learn from each attempt, and keep improving. The market for quality cast products in Africa is growing, and with the right skills, you can be part of it.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To start a small foundry, you need a few essential tools and materials. First, the furnace: you can build a simple charcoal or coke furnace using a 200-litre steel drum lined with refractory clay (a mix of clay, sand, and water). For melting aluminium, a charcoal furnace works well; for iron, you need coke and a forced air supply from a blower or vacuum cleaner. Next, crucibles: clay-graphite crucibles are best for holding molten metal. A #6 or #8 crucible can handle 3-6 kg of aluminium. You'll also need tongs to lift the hot crucible, a skimmer to remove slag, and a pouring shank or ring.

For moulding, you need casting sand. Good sand is fine, slightly damp, and holds shape when squeezed. You can mix silica sand with bentonite clay (about 5-8% by weight) and water. A simple moulding box (flask) made of wood or metal, with a bottom board and a top board, is essential. You'll also need a rammer to pack the sand, a strike-off bar to level it, and a sprue pin to make the pouring hole. For patterns (the shape you want to cast), you can use wood, metal, or even existing parts. A simple pattern like a gear or a pulley can be made from hardwood.

Other tools: a wire brush for cleaning castings, a hacksaw for cutting gates, and a file for finishing. For safety, you need leather gloves, a face shield, a leather apron, and boots. Never pour metal without eye and hand protection. Materials you'll need regularly: scrap metal (aluminium from old pots, car parts; iron from old engine blocks), charcoal or coke, and sand. You can source scrap from local mechanics, junkyards, or households. Keep a stock of sand and clay. With these tools and materials, you're ready to set up a basic foundry. Start small, and upgrade as you earn.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Casting a metal part follows a clear sequence. First, make your pattern. This is a replica of the part you want, slightly larger to allow for shrinkage (about 1% for aluminium, 2% for iron). You can carve it from wood or use an existing part. Next, prepare the mould. Place the pattern in the drag (bottom half of the flask) and fill with sand, ramming it firmly. Flip the drag, place the cope (top half) and the sprue pin, then ram sand in the cope. Remove the sprue pin and pattern, creating a cavity. Cut a pouring basin and vents. Now you have a mould ready for metal.

Melt your metal. Light the furnace and add charcoal or coke. Once hot, place the crucible with scrap metal inside. Use a blower to increase heat. For aluminium, you need about 660Â°C; for iron, 1200-1400Â°C. Watch the metal until it's fully liquid and shiny. Remove slag with a skimmer. Then, pour the molten metal into the mould through the sprue. Pour steadily and continuouslyâdon't stop halfway. Fill the mould completely; you'll see metal rise in the vents. Let it cool. Small parts cool in 10-15 minutes; larger ones may take an hour.

After cooling, break the sand mould and remove the casting. Cut off the sprue and gates with a hacksaw. Grind or file the rough edges. Inspect for defects like holes or cracks. If defective, you can remelt and try again. Finally, finish the part: sand it, paint it, or machine it as needed. Practice this process with simple shapes like a flat bar or a ring. Each step builds skill. Remember, the quality of your mould determines the quality of your casting. Take time to ram sand properly and ensure the pattern is clean. With practice, you'll cast complex parts efficiently.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Even experienced foundry workers make mistakes. Here are common ones and how to fix them. First, mould collapse: if the sand is too dry or not rammed hard enough, the mould walls can fall in when you pour. Fix: mix sand with the right amount of water (it should hold shape when squeezed) and ram it firmly in layers. Second, misrun: when metal cools too quickly and doesn't fill the mould. This happens if the metal isn't hot enough or the mould is too cold. Fix: heat metal until it's fully liquid and preheat the mould slightly (by pouring a little metal and letting it cool, or using a torch). Third, porosity: small holes in the casting due to gas trapped in the metal. This can come from wet sand, dirty scrap, or too much slag. Fix: use dry sand, clean scrap, and skim slag before pouring. Also, add vents to let gas escape.

Fourth, shrinkage: a sunken area where metal contracts as it cools. Fix: add a riser (a reservoir of molten metal) that feeds the casting as it shrinks. Fifth, rough surface: if the sand is too coarse or the pattern is rough, the casting will be rough. Fix: use finer sand and smooth your pattern. Sixth, cold shuts: when two streams of metal meet but don't fuse. This happens if the metal is too cold or pouring is too slow. Fix: pour quickly and continuously with hot metal. Seventh, sand inclusion: sand particles stuck in the casting. Fix: ensure the mould is clean and the sprue is properly designed to avoid turbulence.

Finally, safety mistakes: not wearing protective gear, pouring on wet ground (causes steam explosion), or using wet tools. Always wear leather gloves, face shield, and apron. Pour on dry sand or concrete. Keep a bucket of dry sand to smother fires. If you make a mistake, don't give up. Remelt the metal and try again. Keep a notebook to record what went wrong and what you changed. That's how you improve.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Foundry work is dangerous if you ignore safety. Molten metal can cause severe burns, and fumes can harm your lungs. Always wear proper protective equipment: a face shield (not just goggles), leather gloves, a leather apron, and steel-toed boots. Never wear synthetic clothingâit melts and sticks to skin. Work in a well-ventilated area, preferably outdoors or with a chimney to draw fumes away. When melting scrap, avoid painted, galvanised, or oily metalâthese release toxic fumes. Use only clean scrap.

Before you start, check your equipment. Make sure the crucible is not cracked. Preheat it gradually to avoid thermal shock. Keep the furnace on a stable, non-flammable surface like concrete or bare earth. Clear the area of anything flammable. Have a fire extinguisher or a bucket of dry sand nearby. When pouring, stand to the side, not directly in front of the mould. Pour steadily and avoid splashing. Never pour on wet groundâsteam can explode and throw molten metal. After pouring, let the mould cool completely before opening. Use tongs and gloves to handle hot castings.

Best practices: work with a partner when possible. Have a first-aid kit ready for burns. Keep water away from molten metalâa drop of water can cause an explosion. Store sand and clay in a dry place. Clean your tools after each use. Maintain your furnace: replace lining when worn. Learn to read the metal: when it's ready to pour, it looks like liquid silver and moves easily. Don't rush. Take breaks to avoid fatigue. Remember, safety is not just for youâit's for everyone around you. A safe foundry is a productive foundry.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it's time to put your knowledge into practice. For this exercise, you will cast a simple aluminium keychain or a small flat bar. This will teach you the full process without needing expensive materials. You will need: a small charcoal furnace (or a metal bucket with holes and a blower), a #4 crucible, aluminium scrap (old pots, cans), casting sand, a small wooden pattern (a flat rectangle 5 cm x 2 cm x 1 cm), a two-part flask (or two wooden boxes), and safety gear.

Step 1: Make your pattern from wood. Sand it smooth. Step 2: Prepare the mould. Place the pattern in the drag, fill with sand, and ram it. Flip, place the cope, and ram again. Remove the pattern and cut a sprue hole. Step 3: Melt aluminium in the crucible. Use charcoal and a blower. It should take about 15-20 minutes. Step 4: Pour the molten aluminium into the mould. Be steady. Step 5: Let it cool for 15 minutes. Step 6: Break the mould, remove the casting, and cut off the sprue. File the edges smooth. Congratulationsâyou've made your first casting!

Evaluate your work: Does it have a smooth surface? Are there holes or rough spots? If yes, note what you might change next time (e.g., ram sand harder, use hotter metal). Repeat the exercise to improve. Once you can cast a simple shape reliably, try a more complex pattern like a small gear or a pulley. This exercise is the foundation of your foundry business. With each casting, you build skill and confidence. Soon, you can start selling your products. Keep a record of your pours, including metal temperature, sand mix, and results. That data will help you perfect your craft.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of starting a small foundry in Africa?
options: A) Low demand for cast products
B) High cost of raw materials
C) Availability of scrap metal and local demand
D) Need for expensive imported equipment
quiz.explanation: Scrap metal is readily available and there is high demand for cast parts in local communities.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a common cast product in African markets?
quiz.explanation: Solar panels are not typically produced by small foundries; they are electronic devices.

quiz.q: What is the recommended lining for a simple charcoal furnace?
quiz.explanation: Refractory clay can withstand high temperatures and is used to line furnaces.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a crucible in a small foundry?
quiz.explanation: Clay-graphite crucibles resist thermal shock and are suitable for melting metals.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a sprue pin in moulding?
options: B) To create a pouring hole
quiz.explanation: The sprue pin forms the channel through which molten metal is poured.

quiz.q: What percentage of bentonite clay is typically mixed with silica sand for moulding?
quiz.explanation: About 5-8% bentonite clay by weight provides good bonding for casting sand.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to lift a hot crucible?
quiz.explanation: Tongs are designed to grip and lift crucibles safely.

quiz.q: What is the approximate melting temperature of aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium melts at about 660Â°C, much lower than iron.

quiz.q: Why should you preheat a crucible before use?
quiz.explanation: Preheating prevents cracking due to sudden temperature change.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making a casting?
quiz.explanation: The pattern is needed to form the mould cavity.

quiz.q: How much shrinkage allowance is typical for aluminium castings?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium shrinks about 1% when cooling, so patterns are made slightly larger.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a riser in a mould?
options: B) To feed molten metal as it shrinks
quiz.explanation: A riser acts as a reservoir to compensate for shrinkage during cooling.

quiz.q: Which defect occurs when metal cools too quickly and doesn't fill the mould?
quiz.explanation: Misrun is incomplete filling due to premature solidification.

quiz.q: What causes porosity in castings?
quiz.explanation: Gas bubbles trapped in the metal create pores.

quiz.q: How can you prevent sand inclusion in a casting?
options: B) Ensure clean mould and proper sprue design
quiz.explanation: A clean mould and smooth metal flow reduce sand particles entering the casting.

quiz.q: What should you do if you make a defective casting?
options: D) Use it as a pattern
quiz.explanation: Remelting allows you to reuse the metal and correct mistakes.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to pour molten metal on wet ground?
quiz.explanation: Water turns to steam instantly, causing an explosion that throws molten metal.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT required personal protective equipment for foundry work?
quiz.explanation: Cotton t-shirt does not protect against molten metal; leather or fire-resistant clothing is needed.

quiz.q: What should you do before melting scrap metal?
options: B) Clean it of oil and paint
quiz.explanation: Clean scrap prevents toxic fumes and improves casting quality.

quiz.q: How can you tell when aluminium is ready to pour?
options: B) It looks like liquid silver and moves easily
quiz.explanation: Molten aluminium is shiny and fluid, indicating it is fully melted.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of vents in a mould?
quiz.explanation: Vents allow air and gases to escape, preventing porosity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice when pouring metal?
options: C) Stand directly in front of the mould
quiz.explanation: Continuous pouring prevents cold shuts and ensures a complete fill.

quiz.q: What is the recommended first practical exercise for a beginner?
options: A) Casting a complex engine block
B) Casting a simple flat bar or keychain
quiz.explanation: Simple shapes build foundational skills without high risk or cost.

quiz.q: How long should a small aluminium casting cool before opening the mould?
quiz.explanation: Small castings solidify and cool enough to handle in about 10-15 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a strike-off bar?
options: B) To level sand in the flask
quiz.explanation: A strike-off bar removes excess sand and levels the mould surface.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of a good moulding sand?
options: B) It holds shape when squeezed
quiz.explanation: Good sand has enough moisture and clay to hold its shape when compressed.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid galvanised metal in a foundry?
options: A) It melts at too low a temperature
B) It releases toxic zinc fumes
D) It is difficult to melt
quiz.explanation: Galvanised metal contains zinc, which produces harmful fumes when melted.

quiz.q: What should you keep nearby in case of a fire?
quiz.explanation: Dry sand can smother metal fires; water can cause explosions.

quiz.q: What is the correct sequence for making a casting?
options: A) Melt, mould, pour, cool, finish
B) Mould, melt, pour, cool, finish
C) Pour, melt, mould, cool, finish
D) Cool, melt, pour, mould, finish
quiz.explanation: You prepare the mould before melting and pouring metal.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to keep a notebook in a foundry?
options: B) To track what works and what doesn't
quiz.explanation: Recording details helps you learn from each pour and improve.
